claim: Repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is crucial for genome integrity.
source: Repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) is crucial for genome integrity.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the importance of DSB repair.

claim: A conserved response to DSBs is an increase in chromatin mobility that can be local, at the site of the DSB, or global, at undamaged regions of the genome.
source: A conserved response to DSBs is an increase in chromatin mobility that can be local, at the site of the DSB, or global, at undamaged regions of the genome.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature on chromatin mobility responses to DSBs.

claim: Two types of DSB-induced global chromatin mobility are involved in HR, depending on the position of the DSB.
source: We set up a system that tracks HR in vivo over time and show that two types of DSB-induced global chromatin mobility are involved in HR, depending on the position of the DSB.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data from the THRIV system and mobility measurements.

claim: Close to the centromere, a DSB induces global mobility that depends solely on H2A(X) phosphorylation.
source: Close to the centromere, a DSB induces global mobility that depends solely on H2A(X) phosphorylation and accelerates repair kinetics, but is not essential.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing mobility in H2A-S129A mutants and ChIP data for γ-H2A(X).

claim: Proximal global mobility accelerates repair kinetics but is not essential for HR.
source: Close to the centromere, a DSB induces global mobility that depends solely on H2A(X) phosphorylation and accelerates repair kinetics, but is not essential.
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data showing delayed but eventual repair in H2A-S129A mutants in the C strain.

claim: The global mobility induced by a DSB away from the centromere becomes essential for HR repair.
source: In contrast, the global mobility induced by a DSB away from the centromere becomes essential for HR repair and is triggered by homology search through a mechanism that depends on H2A(X) phosphorylation, checkpoint progression, and Rad51.
evidence: This is supported by data showing lack of HR repair in H2A-S129A and Δrad9 mutants in the S strain.

claim: Distal global mobility is triggered by homology search through a mechanism that depends on H2A(X) phosphorylation, checkpoint progression, and Rad51.
source: In contrast, the global mobility induced by a DSB away from the centromere becomes essential for HR repair and is triggered by homology search through a mechanism that depends on H2A(X) phosphorylation, checkpoint progression, and Rad51.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Δrad9 and Δrad51 mutants showing abolished mobility in the S strain.

claim: Global mobility is governed by chromosomal conformation and differentially coordinates repair by HR.
source: Our data demonstrate that global mobility is governed by chromosomal conformation and differentially coordinates repair by HR.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study, supported by data from different DSB positions (C, L, S strains).

claim: Tel1 and Mec1 are checkpoint kinases that catalyze the phosphorylation of histone H2A in yeast and of H2AX in mammalian cells, forming γ-H2A(X).
source: Two of the most conserved factors contributing to DSB signaling are the checkpoint kinases Tel1 and Mec1 (mammalian ATM/ATR orthologues) that catalyze the phosphorylation of histone H2A in yeast and of H2AX in mammalian cells, forming γ-H2A(X) (Jackson and Bartek, 2009; Waterman et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: γ-H2A(X) extends widely on both sides of the DSB, up to 100 kb in yeast and 1 MB in mammals.
source: γ-H2A(X) extends widely on both sides of the DSB, up to 100 kb in yeast and 1 MB in mammals (Aymard et al., 2017; Caron et al., 2012; Iacovoni et al., 2010; Rogakou et al., 1999; Shroff et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: γ-H2A(X) serves as a docking site for further DDR proteins such as the mediator protein Rad9 (53BP1 in mammals).
source: This wide spreading of γ-H2A(X) serves as a docking site for further DDR proteins such as the mediator protein Rad9 (53BP1 in mammals) (Kinner et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DSBs can be accurately repaired by homologous recombination (HR).
source: DSBs can be accurately repaired by homologous recombination (HR).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DSB repair mechanisms.

claim: HR is predominant in S phase and uses the sister chromatid as template.
source: This mode of repair, predominant in S phase, uses the sister chromatid as template (Symington and Gautier, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Homology search starts with the formation of a presynaptic nucleoprotein filament composed of 3'-ssDNA overhangs coated with the recombinase protein Rad51.
source: Homology search starts with the formation of a presynaptic nucleoprotein filament that is composed of 3'-ssDNA overhangs coated with the recombinase protein Rad51 (Chen et al., 2008; Kalocsay et al., 2009; Sugawara et al., 2003; Wang and Haber, 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The Rad51 nucleofilament enables the sampling and recognition of homology within the nucleus through base pairing.
source: The Rad51 nucleofilament enables the sampling and recognition of homology within the nucleus through base pairing reviewed in Kaniecki et al., 2018.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Rad51 was found strikingly distributed over a large portion of the broken chromosome during homology search.
source: By analyzing Rad51 distribution in haploid yeast after the induction of a single DSB by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP), a study visualized 'snapshots' of ongoing homology search, and found Rad51 strikingly distributed over a large portion of the broken chromosome (Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The genome-wide Rad51 signal distribution was concomitant with that of Mec1-dependent γ-H2A(X).
source: Notably, the genome-wide Rad51 signal distribution was concomitant with that of Mec1-dependent γ-H2A(X), suggesting that Mec1 might be attached on the probing end during homology search.
evidence: This statement is supported by inference from cited literature.

claim: Mec1 might be attached on the probing end during homology search.
source: Notably, the genome-wide Rad51 signal distribution was concomitant with that of Mec1-dependent γ-H2A(X), suggesting that Mec1 might be attached on the probing end during homology search.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on inference from cited data.

claim: Phosphorylation of H2A(X) could promote chromatin remodeling, signaling, or repair.
source: The resulting phosphorylation of H2A(X) could thus promote chromatin remodeling, signaling, or repair.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential functions of H2A(X) phosphorylation.

claim: In budding yeast chromosomes, centromeres are clustered close to the yeast microtubule organizing center (spindle pole body).
source: In the configuration of budding yeast chromosomes (known as the Rabl configuration), centromeres are clustered close to the yeast microtubule organizing center (spindle pole body), as evidenced by abundant trans-contacts between centromeres, and telomeres are bound to the nuclear periphery in a position that depends on the size of the chromosome arms (Duan et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2000; Schober et al., 2008; Therizols et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Telomeres are bound to the nuclear periphery in a position that depends on the size of the chromosome arms.
source: In the configuration of budding yeast chromosomes (known as the Rabl configuration), centromeres are clustered close to the yeast microtubule organizing center (spindle pole body), as evidenced by abundant trans-contacts between centromeres, and telomeres are bound to the nuclear periphery in a position that depends on the size of the chromosome arms (Duan et al., 2010; Jin et al., 2000; Schober et al., 2008; Therizols et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: DSBs recombine more efficiently in spatially proximal regions in yeast.
source: It was shown in yeast that DSBs recombine more efficiently in spatially proximal regions (Agmon et al., 2013; Batté et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Recombination between homologous sequences that lie close to centromeres is more efficient than between regions that are distantly located on chromosome arms.
source: Recombination between homologous sequences that lie close to centromeres is more efficient than between regions that are distantly located on chromosome arms (Agmon et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Induction of a DSB close to a centromere triggers concomitant Rad51 and γ-H2A(X) signals within centromeric regions of all other yeast chromosomes.
source: Accordingly, induction of a DSB close to a centromere triggers concomitant Rad51 and γ-H2A(X) signals within centromeric regions of all other yeast chromosomes, suggesting that homology search can efficiently occur on DNA that is located proximal to the centromere of other chromosomes (Lee et al., 2014; Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Homology search can efficiently occur on DNA that is located proximal to the centromere of other chromosomes.
source: Accordingly, induction of a DSB close to a centromere triggers concomitant Rad51 and γ-H2A(X) signals within centromeric regions of all other yeast chromosomes, suggesting that homology search can efficiently occur on DNA that is located proximal to the centromere of other chromosomes (Lee et al., 2014; Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: Mammalian topologically associated domains (TADs) promote diffusion of ATM, which allows DSB signaling and thus repair.
source: Likewise, mammalian topologically associated domains (TADs), where chromatin contacts are enriched, promote diffusion of ATM, which allows DSB signaling and thus repair (Arnould et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased chromatin mobility, both at the damaged locus (local mobility) and elsewhere in the undamaged genome (global mobility), is a conserved response to DSBs.
source: Originally observed in yeast, increased chromatin mobility, both at the damaged locus (local mobility) and elsewhere in the undamaged genome (global mobility), is a conserved response to DSBs (reviewed in García Fernández and Fabre, 2022; Oshidari et al., 2020; Seeber et al., 2018; Smith and Rothstein, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: Different mechanisms have been described to explain DSB-induced chromatin dynamics, ranging from intrinsic changes in chromatin properties to extrinsic nuclear organizing factors such as actin and microtubules.
source: Different mechanisms have been described to explain these DSB-induced chromatin dynamics, ranging from intrinsic changes in chromatin properties, including chromatin stiffening or decompaction, to extrinsic nuclear organizing factors such as actin and microtubules (Caridi et al., 2018; Hauer et al., 2017; Herbert et al., 2017; Lamm et al., 2020; Lawrimore et al., 2017; Miné-Hattab et al., 2017; Strecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The mobility of damaged and undamaged chromatin has been implicated in various DDR processes such as DSB relocation, clustering, and homology search.
source: Functionally, the mobility of damaged and undamaged chromatin has been implicated in various DDR processes such as DSB relocation, clustering, and homology search.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both local and global mobility allow homology probing in a larger nuclear volume.
source: Several studies have proposed that both types of mobility allow homology probing in a larger nuclear volume (Dion et al., 2012; Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2012; Seeber et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The increase in local and global mobility is abolished in the absence of Rad51 or γ-H2A(X).
source: During homology search, spreading of Rad51 and γ-H2A(X) take place concomitantly and the increase in local and global mobility is abolished in the absence of Rad51 or γ-H2A(X) (García Fernández et al., 2021; Miné-Hattab et al., 2017; Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2012; Smith et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Conflicting results show either a positive correlation between global mobility and recombinant products formation, or a lack of effect of global mobility on recombination in yeast.
source: Conflicting results show either a positive correlation between global mobility and recombinant products formation, or a lack of effect of global mobility on recombination in yeast (Challa et al., 2021; Cheblal et al., 2020; Dion et al., 2012; Hauer et al., 2017; Miné-Hattab et al., 2017; Miné-Hattab and Rothstein, 2012; Strecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature showing conflicting results.

claim: Mobility within a mammalian TAD allows ATM to reach other regions of chromatin and explains the favorable environment for HR observed within a TAD.
source: Similarly, mobility within a mammalian TAD, allowing ATM to reach other regions of chromatin, has also been suggested to explain the favorable environment for HR observed within a TAD (Aymard et al., 2017; Schrank et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mCherry recipient sequence is located on a chromosome under the control of the TEF constitutive promoter and contains an I-SceI cut site followed by a stop codon.
source: The mCherry recipient sequence is located on a chromosome. It is under the control of the TEF constitutive promoter and contains an I-SceI cut site (cs), followed by a stop codon that results in an mCherry truncation.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the THRIV system.

claim: The donor sequence is on a centromeric plasmid and contains an mCherry sequence lacking the promoter and terminator sequences.
source: The donor sequence, is on a centromeric plasmid, hereafter referred to as dCen. It contains an mCherry sequence lacking the promoter and terminator sequences, and shares 539 and 172 bp of homology upstream and downstream of the I-SceI cs of the recipient sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the THRIV system.

claim: The donor sequence shares 539 and 172 bp of homology upstream and downstream of the I-SceI cs of the recipient sequence.
source: The donor sequence, is on a centromeric plasmid, hereafter referred to as dCen. It contains an mCherry sequence lacking the promoter and terminator sequences, and shares 539 and 172 bp of homology upstream and downstream of the I-SceI cs of the recipient sequence (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the THRIV system.

claim: The mCherry recipient sequence was integrated at three different positions: 5 kb from the centromere of chromosome IV (C strain), 400 kb from the centromere (L strain), and 10 kb from the right telomere (S strain).
source: The mCherry recipient sequence was integrated at three different positions: 5 kb from the centromere of chromosome IV, generating the so-called C strain; in a luminal position, 400 kb from the centromere and 1060 kb from the telomere (L strain), and in a subtelomeric position, 10 kb from the right telomere (S strain) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the THRIV system.

claim: All strains have similar doubling time.
source: All strains have similar doubling time (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: I-SceI expression showed a 6.7±0.85-fold increase after 1 hr and a fivefold plateau at longer times.
source: I-SceI expression, measured by RT-qPCR showed a 6.7±0.85-fold increase after 1 hr and a fivefold plateau at longer times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The cutting efficiency was 36%±7.8 at 1 hr and reached 77%±0.8 6 hr after I-SceI induction.
source: The cutting efficiency, measured by qPCRs with primers surrounding the I-SceI cs, was 36%±7.8 at 1 hr and reached 77%±0.8 6 hr after I-SceI induction (Figure 1C), indicating a delay between the enzyme expression and the effective cleavage.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is a delay between I-SceI enzyme expression and effective cleavage.
source: The cutting efficiency, measured by qPCRs with primers surrounding the I-SceI cs, was 36%±7.8 at 1 hr and reached 77%±0.8 6 hr after I-SceI induction (Figure 1C), indicating a delay between the enzyme expression and the effective cleavage.
evidence: This is inferred from the difference in timing between enzyme expression and cutting efficiency.

claim: Increasing I-SceI induction time triggered cell cycle arrest and led to a low number of colonies visible by serial dilutions.
source: Increasing I-SceI induction time triggered cell cycle arrest and led to a low number of colonies visible by serial dilutions.
evidence: This is supported by FACS and serial dilution data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The presence of dCen plasmid resulted in both the resolution of 12 hr cell cycle arrest and recovery of survival after DSB induction.
source: The presence of dCen plasmid resulted in both, the resolution of 12 hr cell cycle arrest and recovery of survival after DSB induction, as shown by FACS analyses and serial dilutions (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is supported by FACS and serial dilution data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Red cells were detected by FACS 4 hr after I-SceI induction and their number progressively increased with time to 87.08±4.43%, 77.40±0.54%, and 72.58±0.42% at 24 hr in C, L, and S strains, respectively.
source: Red cells were detected by FACS 4 hr after I-SceI induction and their number, which included repaired cells and their progeny, progressively increased with time to 87.08±4.43%, 77.40±0.54%, and 72.58±0.42% at 24 hr in C, L, and S strains, respectively (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The lower number of red cells and the lower survival seen in serial dilutions of the S strain could be explained by the greater distance between the DSB near the telomere and the donor sequence.
source: The lower number of red cells and the lower survival seen in serial dilutions of the S strain could be explained by the greater distance between the DSB near the telomere and the donor sequence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial positioning data and repair efficiency data.

claim: The nuclear localization of the dCen plasmid is comparable to that of a pericentromeric sequence.
source: Indeed, the nuclear localization of the dCen plasmid is comparable to that of a pericentromeric sequence (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by distance measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Upon induction by I-SceI in the C strain, the V-Vis locus showed increased dynamic at the short time scale as well as an increased anomalous α.
source: Upon I-SceI induction and generation of a single DSB in the C strain, the V-Vis locus showed increased dynamic at the short time scale as well as an increased anomalous α, indicating changes in chromatin properties around the tracked locus (Figure 2B, +DSB, supplementary file 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary files.

claim: A single DSB in L and S strains had no effect on V-Vis dynamics.
source: In contrast, a single DSB (verified by qPCR, Figure 1C) in L and S strains had no effect on V-Vis dynamics, which remained similar to that observed in the absence of DSB induction (Figure 2B, +DSB).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Global mobility induced by a pericentromeric DSB is not specific to chromosome IV.
source: Global mobility induced by a pericentromeric DSB is not specific to chromosome IV, since I-SceI cs inserted at 7 kb from CENII induced a similar increase in MSDs of the V-Vis locus (Figure 2C, chromosome II, cut).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The increase in global mobility after a DSB in the C strain was observed elsewhere than at the V-Vis locus, on chromosome XIII at 340 and 650 kb from CENXIII.
source: Likewise, the increase in global mobility after a DSB in the C strain was observed elsewhere than at the V-Vis locus, on chromosome XIII at 340 and 650 kb from CENXIII, but to a lesser extent for the locus tracked away from the centromere (Figure 2C, chromosome XIII, tracked).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The spatial position of the DSB plays a key role in induction of global mobility in the absence of homology.
source: Altogether these results show that in the absence of homology, the spatial position of the DSB plays a key role in induction of global mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MSD data from different DSB positions.

claim: A pericentromeric DSB specifically triggers a global mobility that reflects chromatin changes at short times and greater exploration of nuclear space at long times.
source: A pericentromeric DSB specifically triggers a global mobility that reflects chromatin changes at short times and greater exploration of nuclear space at long times (Miné-Hattab et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data and cited literature.

claim: The gradual increase in mobility over the induction time suggests a progressive chromatin change behind global mobility at short times.
source: Furthermore, the gradual increase in mobility over the induction time suggests a progressive chromatin change behind global mobility at short times.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course MSD data.

claim: Before induction, dCen did not alter V-Vis mobility in any of the strains.
source: Before induction, dCen did not alter V-Vis mobility in any of the strains (Figure 2B, -DSB+dCen plasmid).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Upon DSB in the presence of dCen, an increase of V-Vis MSDs was observed even in the L and S strains.
source: Upon DSB, in the presence of dCen, an increase of V-Vis MSDs was now observed even in the L and S strains (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, +DSB+dCen plasmid).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Upon induction of the DSB in the S strain, the closer the donor was to the centromere, the greater the V-Vis mobility was.
source: Upon induction of the DSB in the S strain, the closer the donor was to the centromere, the greater the V-Vis mobility was (Figure 2C, chromosome VII, donor position).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In addition to chromosome architecture, sequence homology is instrumental in inducing global chromatin mobility.
source: These observations highlight that in addition to chromosome architecture, sequence homology is instrumental in inducing global chromatin mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the MSD data with and without donor sequences.

claim: Global mobility may be triggered by homology search only when the DSB is distant from the pericentromeric domain.
source: Global mobility may be triggered by homology search only when the DSB is distant from the pericentromeric domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential mobility patterns observed in different strains.

claim: MSD at 10 s of V-Vis in white cells was higher than that of red cells (0.088 and 0.064, respectively), while cells without DSBs showed limited global mobility (MSD at 10 s of 0.049).
source: MSD at 10 s of V-Vis in white cells was higher than that of red cells (0.088 and 0.064, respectively), while cells without DSBs showed limited global mobility (MSD at 10 s of 0.049) (Figure 3A and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The increase in global chromatin mobility upon DSB induction at pericentromeric site was similar between WT and ∆rad9 cells, regardless of whether dCen was present or not.
source: Surprisingly, the increase in global chromatin mobility upon DSB induction at pericentromeric site was similar between WT and ∆rad9 cells, regardless of whether dCen was present or not (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No increase in global dynamics could be observed in the ∆rad9 mutant when DSB was induced away from the centromere.
source: In contrast, no increase in global dynamics could be observed in the ∆rad9 mutant when DSB was induced away from the centromere, despite effective I-SceI cleavage (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 3C and cleavage efficiency data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Increase in mobility in white cells is not linked to G2/M cell cycle arrest.
source: This indicates that increase in mobility in white cells is not linked to G2/M cell cycle arrest and that the DDR signaling is essential for global mobility only when long-range homology search is required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 mutant data.

claim: DDR signaling is essential for global mobility only when long-range homology search is required.
source: This indicates that increase in mobility in white cells is not linked to G2/M cell cycle arrest and that the DDR signaling is essential for global mobility only when long-range homology search is required.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 mutant data.

claim: HR repair of the DSB generated in the pericentromeric region in the C strain was effective and 40% red cells were obtained after 24 hr of induction in the ∆rad9 mutant.
source: In contrast, HR repair of the DSB generated in the pericentromeric region in the C strain was effective and 40% red cells were obtained after 24 hr of induction (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A G2/M cell cycle arrest is not necessary for the increase in global dynamics and HR repair.
source: These results show that a G2/M cell cycle arrest is not necessary for the increase in global dynamics and HR repair.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 mutant data.

claim: The role of Rad9 signaling in global chromatin dynamics is specific to the position of the DSB.
source: Furthermore, the role of Rad9 signaling in global chromatin dynamics is specific to the position of the DSB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of ∆rad9 in C vs S strains.

claim: Only the mechanism underlying pericentromeric proximal mobility could effectively proceed without Rad9.
source: Indeed, only the mechanism underlying pericentromeric proximal mobility could effectively proceed without Rad9.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 mutant data.

claim: After 6 hr of I-SceI induction, ChIP levels of γ-H2A(X) increased significantly in cis at 50 and 100 kb from the I-SceI CS by approximately 15- and 10-fold in the C and S strains, respectively.
source: After 6 hr of I-SceI induction, ChIP levels of γ-H2A(X) increased significantly in cis at 50 and 100 kb from the I-SceI CS by approximately 15- and 10-fold in the C and S strains, respectively (Figure 4A, white bars).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No increase in ChIP γ-H2A(X) levels was detected at 5 kb from the CS, likely due to 5' to 3' resection occurring from the DSB ends.
source: No increase in ChIP γ-H2A(X) levels was detected at 5 kb from the CS, likely due to 5' to 3' resection occurring from the DSB ends (Eapen et al., 2012; Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on ChIP data and cited literature on resection.

claim: In the presence of the donor, the enrichment of γ-H2A(X) was comparable to that observed with the empty plasmid, except at 100 kb from the cutting site, where a decrease was observed, probably indicating repair.
source: In the presence of the donor, the enrichment of γ-H2A(X) was comparable to that observed with the empty plasmid, except at 100 kb from the cutting site, where a decrease was observed, probably indicating repair (Figure 4A, red bars).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4A, with inference about repair.

claim: In the absence of the donor, enrichment of γ-H2A(X) was observed only if DSB was induced near the centromere (C strain).
source: In the absence of the donor, enrichment of γ-H2A(X) was observed only if DSB was induced near the centromere (C strain).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ChIP levels of γ-H2A(X) increased sixfold in trans at 15 kb and twofold at 50 and 100 kb from CEN-V in the C strain without donor.
source: ChIP levels of γ-H2A(X) increased sixfold in trans at 15 kb and twofold at 50 and 100 kb from CEN-V (Figure 4B, white bars).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The V-Vis locus, located 90 kb from CENV, corresponds to a position where γ-H2A(X) ChIP signals were increased twofold, suggesting a correlation between increased V-Vis mobility and higher γ-H2A(X) levels.
source: Notably, the V-Vis locus, located 90 kb from CENV, corresponds to a position where γ-H2A(X) ChIP signals were increased twofold, suggesting a correlation between increased V-Vis mobility and higher γ-H2A(X) levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between ChIP and mobility data.

claim: An enrichment of γ-H2A(X) ChIP levels was found in trans with a similar increase in both the C and S strains, in the presence of dCen, but not of the empty plasmid.
source: Strikingly, an enrichment of γ-H2A(X) ChIP levels was found in trans with a similar increase in both the C and S strains, in the presence of dCen, but not of the empty plasmid (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of a donor sequence spatially close to the centromere is critical for the propagation of γ-H2A(X) in trans, independently of the genomic position of the DSB.
source: Together, these results reveal that the presence of a donor sequence spatially close to the centromere is critical for the propagation of γ-H2A(X) in trans, independently of the genomic position of the DSB.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP data with and without donor.

claim: γ-H2A(X) spreads around the break and across pericentromeric regions if the DSB is close to the centromere.
source: They further support that γ-H2A(X) spreads around the break and across pericentromeric regions if the DSB is close to the centromere.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP data.

claim: In the H2A-S129A mutant, the increase in global chromatin mobility was similarly impaired in the C and S strains harboring or not the donor sequence dCen.
source: In the H2A-S129A mutant, the increase in global chromatin mobility was similarly impaired in the C and S strains harboring or not the donor sequence dCen (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The MSD curves of the phosphomimetic mutant H2A-S129E showed an increase in both the C and S strains, even in the absence of DNA damage.
source: In contrast, the MSD curves of the phosphomimetic mutant H2A-S129E showed an increase in both the C and S strains, even in the absence of DNA damage (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Global mobility following a single DSB is primarily controlled by H2A(X) phosphorylation, presumably by spreading of this mark.
source: These results clearly indicate that global mobility following a single DSB is primarily controlled by H2A(X) phosphorylation, presumably by spreading of this mark.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the H2A-S129A and H2A-S129E mutant data.

claim: After a DSB generated near the centromere, the kinetics of red cell appearance was reduced in the H2A-S129A mutant compared to the WT, but the number of cells repaired by HR after 24 hr was comparable in both strains.
source: After a DSB generated near the centromere, the kinetics of red cell appearance was reduced in the H2A-S129A mutant compared to the WT, but the number of cells repaired by HR after 24 hr was comparable in both strains (Figure 4D and C, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In the H2A-S129A mutant, a DSB generated in the S strain could not be repaired by HR.
source: In contrast, in the same H2A-S129A mutant, a DSB generated in the S strain could not be repaired by HR (Figure 4D and S, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HR kinetics in the S129E mutant was similar to that in WT strains, regardless of the DSB position.
source: HR kinetics in the S129E mutant was similar to that in WT strains, regardless of the DSB position (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, gray bars).
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: γ-H2A(X)-mediated mobility upon DSB induction is essential to facilitate HR.
source: These results show that γ-H2A(X)-mediated mobility upon DSB induction is essential to facilitate HR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the H2A-S129A mutant data.

claim: The need for mobility and 3D spatial sampling are determined by the position of the DSB and the donor sequence in the nucleus.
source: However, the need for mobility and 3D spatial sampling are determined by the position of the DSB and the donor sequence in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects observed in different strains.

claim: In the absence of a DSB, the global dynamics of WT and ∆rad51 strains were similar.
source: In the absence of a DSB, the global dynamics of WT and ∆rad51 strains were similar (Figure 5B and Figure 5C, -DSB).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Upon I-SceI induction, the ∆rad51 mutant strikingly did not affect the global mobility observed in the C strain.
source: Upon I-SceI induction, the ∆rad51 mutant strikingly did not affect the global mobility observed in the C strain (Figure 5B and Figure 5C, C strain, +DSB).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Deletion of RAD51 abolished the increase in global dynamics induced in the S strain when dCen was present.
source: In contrast, deletion of RAD51 abolished the increase in global dynamics induced in the S strain when dCen was present (Figure 5B and Figure 5C, S strain+DSB+dCen).
evidence: This is supported by MSD data shown in Figure 5B and 5C.

claim: Global mobility could require Rad51 for long-range homology search.
source: These results substantiate that global mobility could require Rad51 for long-range homology search and highlight the existence of a Rad51-independent global mobility when the damage is close to the centromere.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad51 mutant data.

claim: There exists a Rad51-independent global mobility when the damage is close to the centromere.
source: These results substantiate that global mobility could require Rad51 for long-range homology search and highlight the existence of a Rad51-independent global mobility when the damage is close to the centromere.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad51 mutant data.

claim: The position of the DSB, away from or in proximity to the centromeres, engages more or less complex mechanisms for the establishment of global mobility.
source: Hence, the position of the DSB, away from or in proximity to the centromeres, engages more or less complex mechanisms for the establishment of global mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential mechanisms observed in different strains.

claim: All centromeres, anchored at one pole of the nucleus, form a region where trans contacts are enriched.
source: In this chromosome configuration, all centromeres, anchored at one pole of the nucleus, form a region where trans contacts are enriched (Berger et al., 2008; Duan et al., 2010; Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sequences located in territories whose spatial proximity is defined by chromosome organization were shown to be repaired by HR more efficiently than spatially distant regions.
source: Sequences located in territories whose spatial proximity is defined by this chromosome organization were shown to be repaired by HR more efficiently than spatially distant regions, with a striking efficient HR when DSBs were generated in the chromatin close to the centromeres (Agmon et al., 2013; Batté et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Pericentromeric chromatin is particularly enriched in chromosome structural maintenance complexes (SMCs) that include cohesins, condensins, and Smc5/6.
source: This pericentromeric chromatin, corresponding to a 20–50 kb region flanking the 125 bp yeast point centromere (Paldi et al., 2020), is particularly enriched in chromosome structural maintenance complexes (SMCs) that include cohesins, condensins, and Smc5/6.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: SMCs have a strong impact on chromatin loop formation and size.
source: SMCs have a strong impact on chromatin loop formation and size (Betts Lindroos et al., 2006; Dauban et al., 2020; Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Piazza et al., 2021; Weber et al., 2004), further suggesting a link between the particular structure of pericentromeric chromatin and HR repair efficiency.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The repeated emergence of Rabl-like configurations during evolution may point to a functional advantage to centromeric clustering.
source: Interestingly, the recent discovery of the repeated emergence of Rabl-like configurations during evolution may point to a functional advantage to centromeric clustering (Hoencamp et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature.

claim: Proximal mobility correlates with and depends solely on γ-H2A(X) that can spread from the site of damage to other pericentromeric regions.
source: This proximal mobility correlates with and depends solely on γ-H2A(X) that can spread from the site of damage to other pericentromeric regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on ChIP and mobility data.

claim: Proximal mobility is not altered by the presence of a donor sequence, by checkpoint progression, or by the Rad51 nucleofilament.
source: Proximal mobility is not altered by the presence of a donor sequence, by checkpoint progression, or by the Rad51 nucleofilament, as evidenced by the lack of effect of RAD9 (53BP1 ortholog) or RAD51 deletions on mobility, indicating that at least under these conditions, γ-H2A(X) spreading allowed by centromeres clustering is sufficient to enhance chromatin mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 and ∆rad51 mutant data.

claim: γ-H2A(X) spreading allowed by centromeres clustering is sufficient to enhance chromatin mobility.
source: Proximal mobility is not altered by the presence of a donor sequence, by checkpoint progression, or by the Rad51 nucleofilament, as evidenced by the lack of effect of RAD9 (53BP1 ortholog) or RAD51 deletions on mobility, indicating that at least under these conditions, γ-H2A(X) spreading allowed by centromeres clustering is sufficient to enhance chromatin mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the mutant data.

claim: The single DSB generated near a centromere induces DDR activation and H2A phosphorylation, but propagation of γ-H2A(X) through centromeric regions is sufficient to induce global mobility.
source: Here, the single DSB generated near a centromere induces DDR activation and H2A phosphorylation, but propagation of γ-H2A(X) through centromeric regions is sufficient to induce global mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data.

claim: Rad9 could be dispensable because its recruitment remains limited in the regions flanking the DSB.
source: Rad9 could be dispensable because its recruitment remains limited in the regions flanking the DSB (Figure 5; Clouaire et al., 2018; Ferrari et al., 2015; Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on cited literature and the current data.

claim: γ-H2A(X) is primarily induced by the H2A kinase Mec1.
source: γ-H2A(X) is primarily induced by the H2A kinase Mec1 (Lee et al., 2014; Li et al., 2020; Renkawitz et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Proximal mobility is consistent with a model of Mec1 diffusion across centromeres.
source: Our observation that proximal mobility is solely dependent on γ-H2A(X) is consistent with a model of Mec1 diffusion across centromeres.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Mec1 may diffuse in 3D from the site of damage.
source: As suggested by a recent study combining experimental γ-H2A(X) ChIP in the ∆mec1 mutant and mathematical modeling, Mec1 may diffuse in 3D from the site of damage (Li et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The gradual increase in mobility observed in the C strain is consistent with progressive phosphorylation of H2A along the chromosome over time.
source: Although the loop model may not match with the bending properties of yeast chromatin (Li et al., 2020), the gradual increase in mobility we observed in the C strain is consistent with progressive phosphorylation of H2A along the chromosome over time.
evidence: This is an inference based on the time-course mobility data.

claim: Phosphorylation could promote mobility through a stiffer chromatin, due to the repulsion of phosphate negative charges.
source: Whatever the mechanism of propagation, phosphorylation could promote mobility through a stiffer chromatin, due to the repulsion of phosphate negative charges, as we have proposed (García Fernández et al., 2021; Herbert et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on previous work.

claim: H2A phosphorylation could differentially modify chromatin structure by modulating the recruitment of INO80 and SMCs.
source: H2A phosphorylation could also differentially modify chromatin structure by modulating the recruitment of INO80 (Cheblal et al., 2020; Hauer et al., 2017; van Attikum et al., 2004; Bennett et al., 2013), and SMCs (Cheblal et al., 2020; Mirny and Dekker, 2021), or modify the links between microtubules and centromeres, although the loss of centromeric anchoring as a source of global mobility is still debated (Cheblal et al., 2020; Strecker et al., 2016; Lawrimore et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism based on cited literature.

claim: Distal mobility only occurs if a homologous sequence is present and if it is near the centromere.
source: This distal mobility only occurs if a homologous sequence is present and if it is near the centromere.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data with different donor positions.

claim: The donor homologous sequence allows γ-H2A(X) spreading that is the requisite for chromatin motion.
source: We demonstrate that the donor homologous sequence allows γ-H2A(X) spreading that is the requisite for chromatin motion.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP and mobility data.

claim: Distal mobility is dependent on Rad9 and the Rad51 nucleofilament, and is necessary for HR.
source: This distal mobility shares the characteristics of homology search mobility. It is indeed dependent on Rad9 and the Rad51 nucleofilament, and is necessary for HR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ∆rad9 and ∆rad51 mutant data.

claim: Distal mobility shares the characteristics of homology search mobility.
source: This distal mobility shares the characteristics of homology search mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the genetic requirements and behavior of distal mobility.

claim: The presence of a donor is required to observe both H2A phosphorylation and increased distal mobility.
source: The fact that the presence of a donor is required to observe both H2A phosphorylation and increased distal mobility seems to confirm genome sampling by the Rad51 nucleofilament together with Mec1 as proposed by Renkawitz et al., 2014; Renkawitz et al., 2013.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP and mobility data with and without donor.

claim: Recombination would be the cause of distal mobility, in contrast to proximal mobility, which may exist independently of HR.
source: Our observations thus suggest that recombination would be the cause of distal mobility, in contrast to proximal mobility, which may exist independently of HR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential requirements for proximal vs distal mobility.

claim: A DSB involves a cohesin-dependent scaffold of the broken chromosome, which isolates that chromosome from others and inhibits trans contacts.
source: Interestingly, Piazza et al. found that a DSB involves a cohesin-dependent scaffold of the broken chromosome, which isolates that chromosome from others and inhibits trans contacts (Piazza et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Distal mobility could help overcome chromosome isolation and facilitate trans homology searches when needed.
source: The distal mobility we describe here could help overcome this isolation and facilitate trans homology searches when needed.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the current findings and cited literature.

claim: The release of centromeres from their attachment to nuclear microtubules has been suggested as a source of global mobility.
source: The release of centromeres from their attachment to nuclear microtubules emanating from the spindle pole body has been suggested as a source of global mobility (Lawrimore et al., 2017; Strecker et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cytoplasmic microtubule-induced local mobility in Schizosaccharomyces pombe appears to be important for HR repair.
source: On the other hand, cytoplasmic microtubule-induced local mobility in Schizosaccharomyces pombe appears to be important for HR repair (Zhurinsky et al., 2019), and DSB-induced intranuclear microtubules have recently been implicated in directed mobility of the damaged site (Oshidari et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Directed mobilization of damaged DNA involving microtubules, nuclear actin, or nuclear motors has been observed in metazoans.
source: Beyond yeast, directed mobilization of damaged DNA involving microtubules, nuclear actin, or nuclear motors such as myosin and kinesin has been observed in metazoans, pointing to their evolutionary conservation (Caridi et al., 2018; Lamm et al., 2020; Schrank et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Directed motions were involved for the homology-directed repair of DSBs and release of replication stress.
source: Importantly, these directed motions were involved for the homology-directed repair of DSBs and release of replication stress (Caridi et al., 2018; Laflamme et al., 2019; Lamm et al., 2020; Schrank et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: While distal mobility is a product of HR repair, proximal mobility serves as a dispensable booster.
source: Of note, the proximal and distal mobility described here have different roles in HR repair, as documented by directly tracking cells repaired by HR in vivo. While distal mobility is a product of HR repair, proximal mobility serves as a dispensable booster (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HR kinetics data in different mutants.

claim: H2A-S129A mutants are able to form a functional mCherry by HR when the cut is centromere-proximal (C strain), although proximal mobility is not increased.
source: Indeed, H2A-S129A mutants are able to form a functional mCherry by HR, and therefore red colonies, when the cut is centromere-proximal (C strain), although proximal mobility is not increased.
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data in the H2A-S129A mutant.

claim: Red cells appear more slowly in H2A-S129A mutants than in the WT but reach a comparable level between the two strains after 24 hr.
source: Red cells appear more slowly than in the WT but reach a comparable level between the two strains after 24 hr.
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data in the H2A-S129A mutant.

claim: HR can take place without the increase in mobility, but proximal mobility accelerates it.
source: Thus, HR can take place without the increase in mobility, but proximal mobility accelerates it.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the HR kinetics data in the H2A-S129A mutant.

claim: In the C strain deleted for the RAD9 checkpoint gene, red cells surprisingly appear, although there are fewer of them than in the WT strain.
source: Furthermore, in the C strain deleted for the RAD9 checkpoint gene, red cells surprisingly appear, although there are fewer of them than in the WT strain.
evidence: This is supported by HR kinetics data in the ∆rad9 mutant.

claim: Proximal mobility at least partially suppresses the recombination defects associated with the absence of Rad9.
source: This suggests that proximal mobility at least partially suppresses the recombination defects associated with the absence of Rad9.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ∆rad9 mutant data.

claim: The global mobility observed in the H2A-S129E mutant suppresses the ∆rad9 checkpoint defect.
source: This observation is remarkably consistent with our recent findings establishing that the global mobility observed in the H2A-S129E mutant suppresses the ∆rad9 checkpoint defect (García Fernández et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Chromosome organization influences chromatin mobility when damage occurs, which can accelerate repair either by NHEJ or by HR.
source: Chromosome organization influences chromatin mobility when damage occurs, which can accelerate repair either by NHEJ (García Fernández et al., 2021; Ma et al., 2021) or by HR as shown here.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the current study and cited literature.

claim: The global chromatin mobility observed in different regions of the nucleus could be a way to coordinate different responses to DNA damage.
source: The global chromatin mobility observed in different regions of the nucleus could thus be a way to coordinate different responses to DNA damage.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings.

claim: The proximal mobility observed in the pericentromeric region may be an additional mean of ensuring the essential maintenance of centromeres.
source: The proximal mobility observed in the pericentromeric region, in particular, may be an additional mean of ensuring the essential maintenance of centromeres (Yilmaz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the findings and cited literature.

claim: In zebrafish, a link was found between neuronal activity, chromosome mobility, and the number of lesions, highlighting the protective role of chromosome mobility.
source: In zebrafish, a link was found between neuronal activity, chromosome mobility, and the number of lesions, also highlighting the protective role of chromosome mobility.
evidence: This statement is supported by inference from cited literature.

claim: Universally, global mobility would be an additional warrant of genomic integrity.
source: Universally, global mobility would be an additional warrant of genomic integrity.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the findings and broader context.
